```{r, include=FALSE}

Once we have prepared a set of regions for an analysis, we still need to decide
which mobility model to use. Several models may be available for a country, and
a model that fit its original data well may behave quite differently when
applied to new populations and distances. This vignette works through those
choices using the Zambia Facebook models, from inspecting their source data to
comparing predictions and combining them in an ensemble.

All the examples use data included with `nomad`, so you can follow them without
access to the private trip matrices used for fitting. Longer setup and plotting
blocks are folded below their descriptions. Prediction warnings are also kept
in expandable panels beside the relevant result, where you can read how our
example differs from the fitted setting.

```{r}
library(nomad)
```

## Find a relevant source

Let's start by looking at the datasets available for Zambia. Finding data from
the country of interest is useful, but we also need to consider whose movement
was recorded and at what spatial scale. For example, journeys between large
administrative areas may have a different relationship with distance from
journeys between small urban neighbourhoods. The source metadata help us identify
these differences before we compare the fitted models.

The table below includes whether each dataset has fitted models available.
Entries with `has_fitted_models = FALSE` describe data in the catalogue for which
we do not yet have models to use for prediction.

```{r}
mobility_table(country = "ZMB")[, c(
  "name", "aggregation", "has_fitted_models", "prediction_period_days", "distance_unit"
)]
```

We will use `zmb_fb_2025` for the comparison below. Its predictions represent
trip counts over 21 days. This period is separate from the start and end dates
over which the observations were collected. Averaging a series of matrices
retains the 21-day period represented by each matrix, rather than making the
counts refer to the whole collection window.

Datasets and models can be shared through `nomad` even when some of their source
metadata are unavailable. For example, the earlier Zambia Facebook and CDR
models from 2020 do not include a prediction period. Their predicted patterns
of movement can still be explored, but we cannot interpret the counts as trips
per day or convert them to a chosen duration. Looking at metadata completeness
therefore helps us decide which models can support the analysis we have in mind.

## Compare fits to the same observations

Several model families were fit to these observations. We can retrieve them
with `model_table()` and compare their root mean squared error (RMSE), which
summarises the differences between fitted and observed flows. A lower RMSE means
that the model reproduced these particular observations more closely. This is a
useful first comparison, although it does not establish how well that model will
predict movement elsewhere. The table also tells us whether each family supports
prediction for new regions, which we will need later in the example.

```{r}
candidates <- model_table(data_name = "zmb_fb_2025")
knitr::kable(candidates[, c("model_type", "mobility_model", "RMSE", "max_rhat", "supports_newdata")],
             digits = 2, col.names = c("Type", "Family", "RMSE", "Maximum R-hat", "New regions"))
```

Before choosing the model with the smallest error, it is also useful to look at
`max_rhat`. R-hat compares variation within and between the chains used to fit the
model. A high value raises a concern that the chains have not converged, so the
reported parameter estimates need further review even if the fit error is small.
The package preserves the supplied fits and flags values above 1.1 through
`rhat_above_1_1`. You can inspect individual parameters with `summary(model)`;
being below the flag threshold does not by itself establish that a fit is reliable.

We can use the available RMSE values to calculate a set of model weights. The
chosen statistic needs to be available for every model in the comparison.
For example, the deviance information criterion (DIC) was not calculated for
these fits, so we cannot use it to derive their weights.

These fit-based weights are most interpretable when the models were fit to
the same observations. Across different datasets, differences in trip counts,
spatial aggregation and sampling can change the scale of the errors. Combining
those errors would then mix differences in the data with differences in model
performance. For this reason, `model_weights()` requires the models to share a
source dataset. If we want to compare models from different sources, we can choose
manual weights and examine how our results change across those choices, making
clear that the weights describe a sensitivity analysis.

```{r}
weights <- model_weights(data_name = "zmb_fb_2025", metric = "RMSE")
knitr::kable(weights[, c("name", "RMSE", "weight")], digits = c(0, 1, 3))
```

For these fits, the RMSE weights are proportional to the inverse error and
normalised to sum to one. A model with half the error of another therefore
receives twice its weight. This summarises relative fit to the Zambia
observations, but does not tell us how similar our prediction setting is to
the source setting or give a probability that each model is correct. We will
therefore inspect the models and their predictions before deciding how to
combine them.

## Inspect the source and diagnostics

For the rest of this example we will compare normalised exponential gravity with
exponential departure-diffusion, both fit to `zmb_fb_2025`. Each has a stored
maximum R-hat of 1.01 and minimum effective sample sizes above 600. The effective
sample size accounts for similarity between successive draws, so it can be much
smaller than the number of samples stored. These summaries help us choose
examples with more reassuring sampling diagnostics, although a full convergence
assessment would also require inspecting the chains themselves.

We can use `model_profile()` to see the distance units, population scale and
prediction period associated with a model. The saved fit checks then let us
compare its predictions with the original observations, even though the private
trip matrix itself is not distributed with the package.

```{r}
gravity <- model_db$zmb_fb_2025_mod_grav_exp_norm
departure <- model_db$zmb_fb_2025_mod_dd_exp
model_profile(gravity)
check(gravity, plots = FALSE)
```

```{r, fig.width=8, fig.height=4, fig.alt="Observed and fitted flows for Zambia exponential gravity"}
plot(gravity)
```

In the observed-versus-predicted panel, flows near the line of agreement are
those the model reproduces closely. Look for groups of flows that are consistently
overpredicted or underpredicted, and for patterns in the residual panel. For
example, a model might fit the largest flows reasonably well while missing many
small ones, which could matter when studying movement into less connected areas.

These checks describe the source fit. Before using it for our own regions, we
also need to check whether their distances and populations are comparable, and
whether the model can accept the inputs we want to provide. The next step sets
up a small prediction request so we can work through those checks.

## Prepare a common prediction setting

To keep the matrices small enough to inspect, we will use eight regions from the
distances and populations used for fitting. The distance matrix `D` has origins in its rows and destinations
in its columns, while `N` gives the population of each region. We keep the region
names on both inputs so that `nomad` can match the populations to the correct
rows and columns. For your own analysis, these would be the distances and
population estimates prepared for your study regions.

```{r, fold_label="Show how to construct the common regions"}
source <- gravity$get_model()$data
regions <- rownames(source$D)[1:8]
newdata <- list(
  D = source$D[regions, regions],
  N = source$N_orig[regions]
)
```

The source distances are measured in metres, so we supply `unit = "m"` when
predicting. This tells `nomad` how to interpret our input distances. It can then
convert them to the units used by each fitted model, which is particularly useful
when comparing models whose original data used different units.

Although we have kept the source populations for these eight regions, we have
removed the remaining regions from the prediction setting. The warnings about
fewer regions and a smaller total population draw attention to this change.
For a model that distributes movement across the available destinations,
removing destinations can change the remaining flows. These predictions therefore
describe a new, smaller setting; they should not be treated as simply extracting
eight rows and columns from a prediction for the full source population.

```{r}
a <- predict(gravity, newdata = newdata, unit = "m", duration = 21)
b <- predict(departure, newdata = newdata, unit = "m", duration = 21)
round(a[1:4, 1:4])
```

Each entry is a predicted trip count from its row region to its column region
over 21 days. The counts can include repeated trips by the same person. If we
requested 42 days, the package would double these values, assuming the same average daily trip rate throughout.
That conversion cannot describe seasonal changes or changes in travel behaviour.

This conversion depends on having a source prediction period. For models shared
without that information, leaving `duration` unset returns the unscaled
prediction with a warning. Requesting a conversion instead raises an error,
since the package cannot calculate the multiplier. Such a model may still help
us explore relative movement, but we would need the missing metadata before
using its predictions as trip counts over a specified period.

## Recognise unsupported requests

Basic and finite radiation models retain predictions for their exact original
regions and populations. They cannot transfer the stored matrix to the eight-region
subset above. `nomad` rejects that request directly, including through an
ensemble, and explains how to choose a model that supports new regions or
recalculate radiation with `mobility` when you have the necessary trip totals.
For the original regions, we can retrieve the stored prediction without
supplying new inputs, as below.

```{r}
radiation <- model_db$zmb_fb_2025_mod_rad_basic
original <- predict(radiation)
dim(original)
```

For model families that support new inputs, a different country, spatial scale
or population may still be a valid prediction request. The warnings identify
those differences so that we can consider whether transferring the fitted
parameters is reasonable. Country checks require `locations`, supplied as an
`sf` object or a longitude/latitude table, because distances alone do not locate
the regions geographically. None of the bundled models was fit to international
travel, so a prediction between countries would require assumptions beyond what
those source data can establish.

## Inspect uncertainty

The predictions above use the mean estimates of the fitted parameters. To explore
how the stored parameter uncertainty affects the predicted flows, we can request
100 simulations with `nsim = 100`. For a model that supports these simulations,
the result is an array containing one mobility matrix per draw. We can then use
`uncertainty_summary()` to look at quantities such as the total number of trips
and the number travelling between different regions.

The current `mobility` predictor samples each parameter independently from a
normal distribution truncated at zero, using its stored mean and standard
deviation. The draws therefore approximate the uncertainty in each parameter
separately. They do not preserve relationships between parameters in the original
Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samples. These predictions also leave out
observation noise, uncertainty in populations or distances, and uncertainty
about applying the model in another setting.

```{r}
draws <- predict(gravity, newdata = newdata, unit = "m", nsim = 100, seed = 42)
uncertainty_summary(draws, metrics = c("total", "between_region", "max"))
selected <- uncertainty_matrices(draws, metric = "between_region", probs = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))
attr(selected, "selected")
```

To visualise the variation, we select draws near the 10th, 50th and 90th
percentiles of between-region movement. Each selected matrix comes from one
complete draw, preserving the pattern of flows that its parameters produced.
Taking a separate quantile in every cell could instead assemble a matrix that
was never predicted by any one parameter draw. If we ranked by a different
quantity, such as the largest individual flow, we might select different matrices.

The three heatmaps use a common colour scale so that a given colour means the
same number of trips in each panel. The scale uses log(1 + trips), allowing both
large and small flows, including zeros, to remain visible.

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.5, fig.alt="Lower, median and upper mobility matrices selected by between-region movement"}
plot_uncertainty(draws, metric = "between_region", probs = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))
```

The small difference between these panels is present in the supplied fit. We can
check its parameter summaries and quantify the spread in between-region trips:

```{r}
parameter_summary <- gravity$get_model()$summary[, c("mean", "sd")]
parameter_summary
between <- mobility_metrics(draws)$between_region
interval <- stats::quantile(between, c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))
relative_width <- 100 * (interval[3] - interval[1]) / interval[2]
```

For these 100 draws, the 10th-to-90th percentile interval is only
`r sprintf("%.3f%%", relative_width)` of the median between-region trip total.
The movement-rate parameter `theta` and distance parameter `delta` have very
small stored standard deviations relative to their means. In this normalised
gravity model, total trips are `theta * sum(N)`, which also constrains variation
in the total. The destination-population exponent `omega` is close to zero, so destination
population contributes little to differences between flows in this fit.

The narrow spread therefore reflects the stored parameter summaries and the
prediction method for this particular fitted model. It would be misleading to
interpret it as the full uncertainty about travel in these regions, since it
omits the other sources described above. Increasing `nsim` would estimate the
same approximate distribution more precisely, but would not account for those
missing sources. To investigate uncertainty about model choice, we can instead
compare the predictions from different plausible models, as in the next section.

## Compare and combine predictions

We now have two predictions for the same target regions and period, so we can
compare their entries directly. Using gravity as the baseline, a positive value
from `prediction_difference(b, a)` means that departure-diffusion predicts more
trips for that origin-destination pair. The function matches region names if
their order differs, and raises an error if the matrices refer to different
sets of target regions.

We can also combine the two models in an ensemble. The example below gives 60%
of the weight to gravity and 40% to departure-diffusion, then compares the total
predicted trips with those from each component.

```{r}
round(prediction_difference(b, a)[1:4, 1:4])
ensemble <- nomad_ensemble(list(gravity = gravity, departure = departure),
                           weights = c(gravity = 0.6, departure = 0.4))
combined <- predict(ensemble, newdata = newdata, unit = "m", duration = 21)
c(gravity = sum(a), departure = sum(b), ensemble = sum(combined))
```

Here the weights are choices we have made for the example. We could give the
models equal influence or calculate fit-based weights for these two models,
provided we are satisfied that their fit statistics are an appropriate basis
for the comparison. The weights calculated earlier included every model for the
dataset, so we would need to restrict that calculation to the components we
intend to combine.

To see how those choices affect individual flows, compare three fixed weights
against the gravity prediction. Each panel below shows **ensemble minus gravity**:
red cells mean more trips than gravity predicts, blue cells mean fewer, and white
means no change. Rows are origins and columns are destinations, including trips
that stay within the same region on the diagonal.

All panels use the same colour limits, centred on zero. The weights are illustrative
sensitivity choices, not estimates of which model is correct. With two fixed
component matrices, the difference is `weight * (departure - gravity)`, so the
pattern stays the same while its magnitude changes. Here `weight` is the share
given to departure-diffusion.

```{r weight-differences, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.5, fold=TRUE, fold_label="Show how to compare fixed ensemble weights", fig.alt="Difference from gravity predictions at 25, 50 and 75 percent departure-diffusion weight; red means more trips and blue means fewer, with one shared colour scale"}
weights <- c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)
differences <- lapply(weights, function(weight) {
  candidate <- nomad_ensemble(list(gravity = gravity, departure = departure),
                              weights = c(gravity = 1 - weight, departure = weight))
  prediction <- predict(candidate, newdata = newdata, unit = "m", duration = 21)
  cells <- as.data.frame(as.table(prediction_difference(prediction, a)))
  names(cells) <- c("origin", "destination", "difference")
  cells$weight <- paste0(100 * weight, "% departure-diffusion")
  cells
})
changes <- do.call(rbind, differences)
changes$origin <- factor(changes$origin, levels = rev(rownames(a)))
changes$destination <- factor(changes$destination, levels = colnames(a))
limit <- max(abs(changes$difference))

ggplot2::ggplot(changes, ggplot2::aes(destination, origin, fill = difference)) +
  ggplot2::geom_tile() +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~weight, nrow = 1) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
    midpoint = 0, limits = c(-limit, limit),
    labels = function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_discrete(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_discrete(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Destination", y = "Origin", fill = "Change in predicted trips") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    panel.grid = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5),
    strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.5, "cm")
  )
```

The heatmaps show which flows are most affected by changing the ensemble weights.
Whether those differences matter will depend on what we use the mobility matrix
for. For example, a modest difference in travel to a less connected region might
change when an outbreak reaches it, even if the total number of trips changes
very little. The [outbreak example](outbreak-model-selection.html) takes this next
step by comparing daily incidence under several mobility assumptions while
keeping the transmission parameters fixed.
